practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a wasting process?
A) Injection moulding
B) Vacuum forming
C) Drilling
D) Brazing
practice_questions.marks: C) Drilling [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two process types that change the shape of a material without removing any material from the workpiece.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: shaping / forming / additive / joining (accept any two that correctly do not involve material removal). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why drilling a hole in a metal block is classified as a wasting process.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying it as wasting; 1 mark for stating material is removed from the workpiece; 1 mark for a developed point such as the removed material becomes waste swarf that is not part of the finished component, or that the starting block must be larger than the finished part. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by an additive manufacturing process. Give one example of a product that would be suitable for this process.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a process that builds up a product layer by layer from a digital model, adding material only where it is needed / produces virtually no waste (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'it adds material'). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, a prototype engineering component or a custom bracket produced by FDM 3D printing, with a reason why it suits that process — such as complex geometry, one-off production, or no tooling required (2 marks for a specific applied example with justification; 1 mark for naming a product without justification). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer needs to produce 10,000 identical plastic housings for an electric motor. The housings have a complex internal cavity.

Discuss which process type or types would be most appropriate for manufacturing the housings at this scale.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two process types, with specific reasoning applied to the scenario. For example: shaping via injection moulding suits high volumes and complex cavities — the mould is expensive but amortised over 10,000 units, giving low unit cost; contrasted with additive manufacturing, which could produce the complex cavity but is far too slow and costly at this volume. A clear recommendation is reached with justification.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two process types identified with some reasoning linked to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One process type identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A design engineer is evaluating whether to use a wasting process or a forming process to manufacture a steel bracket from a solid billet.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of each process type for this application, and justify which you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation addressing at least two advantages and one disadvantage of each process type, applied to the steel bracket scenario. Wasting advantages: high dimensional precision, smooth surface finish, suits complex shapes; disadvantages: material waste, higher material cost. Forming advantages: no material waste, can improve grain structure and mechanical properties, efficient for high volume; disadvantages: high tooling cost for dies, limited to simpler shapes compared to multi-axis wasting. A substantiated recommendation is reached — for example, forming (forging) is preferable for high-volume production of a safety-critical bracket due to improved grain structure and lower unit cost, but wasting is preferable for a one-off prototype needing tight tolerances.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two relevant points on each process type with some application to the scenario and an attempted recommendation.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points made but largely one-sided or without a recommendation.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about one process type, no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a shaping process?
A) Turning
B) Forging
C) Sand casting
D) Powder coating
practice_questions.marks: C) Sand casting [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two safety measures that must be followed when using a pillar drill.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: clamp the workpiece securely to the table / wear safety glasses / keep loose clothing and hair away from the drill / select the correct speed for the material / clear swarf with a brush not fingers / lower the guard before drilling. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why die casting is more suitable than sand casting for producing 50,000 identical aluminium components.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that die casting uses a permanent reusable steel die; 1 mark for explaining that this makes unit cost low at high volume; 1 mark for a developed point such as die casting achieves better dimensional accuracy and surface finish than sand casting, reducing finishing costs — or that the high initial die cost is amortised over 50,000 units, giving a lower cost per part than making a new sand mould for each casting. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the steps involved in the FDM 3D printing process. Include the tools and equipment required.
practice_questions.marks: Steps (up to 2 marks): slice the digital model in software into layers; load filament spool; FDM printer melts filament in heated nozzle; deposits material layer by layer onto build platform; platform lowers by one layer after each pass; support structures removed after printing (2 marks for a logical sequence covering at least three steps; 1 mark for a basic description). Equipment (up to 2 marks): FDM 3D printer, slicing software, thermoplastic filament spool (e.g. PLA or ABS); optionally: removal tools for supports (2 marks for naming at least two items; 1 mark for one). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer is deciding between MIG welding and bolted mechanical fastening to join the steel side panels of a heavy-duty storage cabinet.

Discuss the factors that should influence this choice of joining method.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two factors from each process with specific reasoning. For example: MIG welding produces a strong permanent joint suitable for the structural load, gives a clean appearance, but requires skilled operators and PPE and cannot be disassembled for repair; bolting allows disassembly for maintenance or replacement, requires less skill, but creates stress concentrations at bolt holes and may loosen under vibration. A clear recommendation is reached with justification linked to the storage cabinet scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two factors identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two factors mentioned with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A student is planning to manufacture a prototype housing for an electronic sensor. The housing has a complex curved outer surface and a hollow interior.

Evaluate the suitability of vacuum forming and FDM 3D printing for manufacturing this prototype, and justify which process you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Balanced evaluation covering vacuum forming (suits curved surfaces, fast cycle, low cost per part, but requires a mould and cannot produce hollow interiors in one operation, draft angles limit deep vertical walls) and FDM (builds hollow complex geometry directly from the digital model, no tooling cost, but slower, lower surface finish, limited material choice). Judgement should favour FDM for a one-off prototype with complex hollow geometry because no mould cost, digital iteration is fast, and accuracy is adequate for a sensor housing. Judgement should be substantiated and acknowledge counterpoints.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two relevant points on each process and an attempted recommendation.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points identified but largely one-sided or without justification.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a thermosetting polymer?
A) ABS
B) Polycarbonate
C) Epoxy resin
D) PLA
practice_questions.marks: C) Epoxy resin [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two properties of stainless steel that make it suitable for use in food processing machinery.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: corrosion resistant / does not rust / easy to clean / hygienic / hard / strong / tough. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a thermoplastic and a thermosetting polymer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that thermoplastics soften when heated and harden on cooling (reversible); 1 mark for stating that thermosets undergo irreversible chemical cross-linking on curing and cannot be re-melted; 1 mark for a developed point such as thermoplastics can be recycled by remelting whereas thermosets cannot, or thermoplastics are used in injection moulding because they can be repeatedly melted. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the properties of carbon reinforced polymer (CRP). Give one application where these properties make it the most suitable material choice.
practice_questions.marks: Properties (up to 2 marks): very high strength-to-weight ratio / stiff and strong / lightweight / corrosion-resistant / can be formed into complex shapes (2 marks for two distinct properties; 1 mark for one). Application (up to 2 marks): for example, aerospace structural panels or racing car body/chassis, because the high strength-to-weight ratio reduces overall mass while maintaining structural integrity at high load, which improves fuel efficiency or performance (2 marks for a specific application with justification linking properties to requirements; 1 mark for naming an application without justification). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A product designer is selecting a polymer for a transparent outdoor safety shield that must resist impact and UV degradation.

Discuss which polymer from the specification would be most appropriate, justifying your answer with reference to material properties.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion considering at least two polymer candidates and evaluating their suitability. For example: polycarbonate — extremely tough, optically clear, suitable outdoors with UV stabiliser added; PMMA/acrylic — optically clear but significantly more brittle than polycarbonate and can crack under impact, less suitable for a safety shield. A clear justified recommendation for polycarbonate is reached, acknowledging that polycarbonate is more expensive but that its impact resistance is critical for safety applications.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two polymers compared with some reasoning linked to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One polymer identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Smart materials are increasingly used in engineering manufacture.

Evaluate the advantages and limitations of using smart materials compared with conventional engineering materials in manufactured products. Use specific examples of smart materials in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Balanced evaluation with at least two named smart materials, their stimuli and responses, specific applications, and a comparison against conventional alternatives. Advantages: respond autonomously without external control systems (e.g. SMA orthodontic wires self-correct as they warm); enable miniaturisation (QTC pressure sensors replace mechanical switch components); can be embedded in products for sensing functions (thermochromic packaging). Limitations: more expensive than conventional materials; properties are temperature/stimulus-sensitive so may behave unpredictably in extreme environments; limited range of available materials; some (e.g. Nitinol SMA) are difficult to machine using conventional wasting processes. A substantiated judgement is given — e.g. smart materials offer significant functional advantages but are best suited to high-value applications where their autonomous response justifies the cost premium.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two smart materials named and compared with conventional alternatives, some limitations, attempted judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): One smart material described but limited comparison or evaluation.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which property describes the ability of a material to return to its original shape after the applied force is removed?
A) Ductility
B) Hardness
C) Elasticity
D) Malleability
practice_questions.marks: C) Elasticity [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two mechanical properties of a material that would be important when selecting a metal for a vehicle suspension spring.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: elasticity (must return to original shape after deflection) / high yield strength (must not permanently deform under load) / toughness (must resist fatigue cracking under cyclic loading). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between ductility and malleability.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining ductility as the ability to be permanently deformed under tension (drawn into wire) without fracturing; 1 mark for defining malleability as the ability to be permanently deformed under compression (hammered or rolled into shape) without fracturing; 1 mark for a developed point such as both describe plastic deformation without fracture but ductility involves a tensile force while malleability involves a compressive force — or giving a material example for each (copper for ductility; lead or mild steel for malleability). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the machinability of a material. Give one example of a metal with high machinability and one with low machinability.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): machinability describes how easily a material can be cut, drilled or machined — a material with high machinability can be processed at high cutting speeds with low cutting forces, good surface finish and reasonable tool life (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement). Examples (1 mark each): high machinability — brass or aluminium (1 mark); low machinability — stainless steel, because it work-hardens during cutting and rapidly dulls cutting tools (1 mark). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer is selecting a material for the blade of a hand chisel. The blade must resist being scratched or chipped on the cutting edge but must also be able to absorb occasional impact loads without shattering.

Discuss which mechanical properties are most important for this application and how they might conflict.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying hardness (resists scratching/indentation on the cutting edge, required to maintain sharpness) and toughness (absorbs impact energy without fracturing, required when the chisel strikes a knot or is used with a mallet) as the two key properties, and explicitly addressing their conflict — harder materials tend to be more brittle (lower toughness); a very hard blade may hold its edge but shatter under impact. The discussion should consider how manufacturers resolve this — for example, using high carbon steel at the correct heat-treated temper, or composite tools with a hard carbide tip bonded to a tough steel body. A reasoned recommendation is made.
Secure (3–4 marks): Both properties identified with some reasoning about the conflict.
Developing (2 marks): One property identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A student is deciding between aluminium alloy and stainless steel for a bespoke bracket that requires extensive CNC milling. The bracket will be used outdoors and must withstand moderate tensile loads.

Evaluate the suitability of each material for this application with reference to relevant material properties, and justify which you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Balanced evaluation addressing at least three properties for each material, applied to the specific scenario. Aluminium — high machinability (fast CNC milling, lower tool wear, cheaper manufacturing), good corrosion resistance outdoors, low density, adequate tensile strength for moderate loads; limitations: lower tensile strength than stainless steel per unit area. Stainless steel — high tensile and compressive strength, excellent corrosion resistance, but low machinability (work-hardening causes rapid tool wear, longer cycle times, higher manufacturing cost). Recommendation should acknowledge the trade-off: aluminium alloy is preferred for a bespoke one-off CNC-milled bracket because the machinability advantage significantly reduces manufacturing cost, corrosion resistance is adequate outdoors, and the moderate load requirement is met by a suitable aluminium alloy grade. Stainless steel would be preferred only if tensile loads were high or the part required food-contact certification. Judgement is substantiated.
Secure (5–6 marks): Three or more relevant points on each material with a reasoned recommendation.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points made but largely one-sided or without clear justification.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a consideration under 'sustainability' when selecting an engineering material?
A) The colour and surface texture of the material
B) The availability of the material from multiple suppliers
C) The energy required to recycle the material at end of life
D) The cutting speed achievable when machining the material
practice_questions.marks: C) The energy required to recycle the material at end of life [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two factors, other than mechanical properties, that an engineer must consider when selecting a material for a manufactured component.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: cost (material or manufacturing) / availability / aesthetics / sustainability / machinability / form of supply. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why availability of a material is an important consideration in engineering manufacture.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a material must be obtainable in the required stock form; 1 mark for a point about lead time or supply certainty (e.g. a long lead time can delay production; a single supplier creates supply-chain risk); 1 mark for a developed point such as even if a material has ideal properties, it is not a practical choice if it cannot be delivered in sufficient quantity and in the correct section within the required production schedule. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how cost influences material selection. Include both material cost and manufacturing cost in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Material cost (up to 2 marks): the price of raw stock per kilogram or standard section — a lower material cost reduces the unit cost per component; for example, low carbon steel is far cheaper per kg than titanium (2 marks for a developed explanation with example; 1 mark for a basic statement). Manufacturing cost (up to 2 marks): the tooling, energy and labour required to process the material — a material with high machinability (e.g. aluminium) reduces machining time and tool wear costs; a material with poor machinability (e.g. stainless steel) increases cycle time and tooling cost (2 marks for a developed explanation with example; 1 mark for a basic statement). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer is selecting a material for the outer casing of a portable electronic device. The casing must protect internal components from impact, be visually attractive, and be produced at low cost in high volumes.

Discuss which material selection criteria are most relevant to this application and identify a suitable candidate material.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least three relevant criteria applied to the scenario. Properties — impact resistance is critical; a brittle material such as acrylic or cast iron would be eliminated. Cost — high volume justifies injection moulding tooling cost; a thermoplastic with high machinability reduces manufacturing cost. Aesthetics — the casing is visible and contributes to product appeal; material should accept surface texturing and colouring. A named candidate — for example ABS — is justified: tough, impact-resistant, easy to injection mould at high volume, readily coloured and textured. Sustainability noted as a possible limitation (petroleum-derived, non-biodegradable). A clear recommendation is reached.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two criteria discussed with some application and a candidate material named.
Developing (2 marks): One criterion identified with a material named but limited justification.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A civil engineer is choosing between low carbon steel and aluminium alloy for a structural bracket that will be used outdoors on a coastal building. The bracket must carry significant loads, will be highly visible, and must last at least 25 years with minimal maintenance.

Evaluate the suitability of each material for this application against all relevant selection criteria, and justify which you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Balanced evaluation covering at least four criteria for each material applied to the scenario. Properties: low carbon steel has higher tensile strength but corrodes rapidly in a coastal (salt-laden) environment without regular painting; aluminium alloy has lower density, adequate structural strength for moderate loads, and excellent corrosion resistance without maintenance coatings. Cost: steel is cheaper per kg; aluminium is more expensive but eliminates recurring maintenance cost. Availability: both widely stocked. Aesthetics: aluminium can be anodised for an attractive durable coloured finish; steel must be painted repeatedly. Sustainability: both recyclable, but aluminium uses more energy in primary smelting; steel's global recycling rate is higher. Recommendation: aluminium alloy is preferred for a coastal structural bracket because its inherent corrosion resistance eliminates painting maintenance (a significant lifetime cost), adequate strength is achievable with appropriately sized sections, and its aesthetic finish is more durable — despite higher initial material cost. Counterpoint acknowledged: if loads were very high, steel's superior tensile strength might be decisive. Judgement is substantiated.
Secure (5–6 marks): Three or more criteria covered with a reasoned recommendation.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points made but limited to one or two criteria or no recommendation.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes batch production?
A) Making a single unique item to a customer's exact specification
B) Manufacturing a set quantity of identical products before reconfiguring the machines
C) Continuous high-volume production of standardised products
D) Using a robot to assemble components automatically
practice_questions.marks: B) Manufacturing a set quantity of identical products before reconfiguring the machines [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using jigs and fixtures in batch production.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: improved dimensional consistency / reduced marking-out time / faster cycle times / reduced skill requirement per operation / greater repeatability between parts. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why mass production results in a lower unit cost than one-off production.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that high volume spreads fixed costs. Second mark for developing this — e.g. the capital cost of dedicated tooling and automated machinery is divided across a very large number of units, reducing cost per part. Third mark for a further point — e.g. cycle time is very short because machines run continuously without reconfiguration, so labour cost per unit is minimal. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by CAM (computer-aided manufacture) and give one example of how it improves the quality of manufactured parts.
practice_questions.marks: Description (2 marks): CAM involves using software to generate toolpaths that are downloaded to a CNC machine, which then drives cutting tools automatically without the operator controlling each movement during the cut. Example (2 marks): for example, a CNC milling machine following a CAM program will produce every pocket to exactly the same depth and position on every component in a batch, eliminating the dimensional variation that would occur if an operator set each depth manually. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A company is deciding whether to invest in fully automated robotic assembly for its production line, which currently uses manual operators.

Discuss the advantages and limitations of switching to fully automated robotic control.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two advantages (e.g. robots can operate continuously without fatigue, operate in hazardous environments such as spray-paint booths, and produce consistent output at high rates) and at least two limitations (e.g. very high initial capital outlay, significant reduction in employment opportunities for skilled operators, downtime if the robotic system fails), with each point developed and linked to the production context.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant points on each side, briefly explained.
Developing (2 marks): One advantage and one limitation identified but not developed.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A small engineering company manufactures custom motorcycle frames. Each frame is designed to the rider's exact body measurements and riding style. Currently the company is considering whether to move to batch production of standard frame sizes.

Evaluate the extent to which moving from one-off to batch production would benefit this company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies genuine benefits of batch production (lower unit cost through jig use and reduced setup time per unit, more predictable lead times, easier stock management), then challenges these with specific reasons why one-off production may remain the better choice for this company (custom frames lose the unique selling point of bespoke fit; standard sizes may not suit all customers; investment in jigs for each standard size still carries cost; the company's skilled workforce is its competitive advantage). A clear, substantiated judgement is reached — e.g. batch production offers cost benefits only if customer demand for standard sizes exists, which must be validated before investment.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides covered with some application to the motorcycle frame context and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided or lacking judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about one-off or batch with little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes quality assurance?
A) Measuring and inspecting parts after they have been manufactured
B) Rejecting parts that fall outside the permitted tolerance
C) Putting systems and procedures in place to prevent defects occurring
D) Using a micrometer to check shaft diameters against a specification
practice_questions.marks: C) Putting systems and procedures in place to prevent defects occurring [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why an engineering company would implement a quality system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: early intercept of problems in production / reducing waste and associated costs / consistency of finished products / conformity to industry standards and regulations / reducing issues at the customer and returns. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A shaft is dimensioned on an engineering drawing as 30 mm ± 0.1 mm. Explain what this means and calculate the maximum and minimum acceptable dimensions.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for explaining that the dimension must fall within an acceptable range centred on 30 mm. Second mark: maximum acceptable = 30 + 0.1 = 30.1 mm. Third mark: minimum acceptable = 30 − 0.1 = 29.9 mm. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between quality control and quality assurance. Give one example of a quality control activity in an engineering factory.
practice_questions.marks: Description (2 marks): QC is a reactive approach where parts are measured and inspected after manufacture to detect defects; QA is a preventative approach where systems are put in place to reduce the chance of defects occurring (2 marks for a clear contrast of both; 1 mark if only one is described). Example (2 marks): a QC activity could be using a go/no-go gauge at the end of a CNC turning operation to check that every shaft diameter is within the stated tolerance before the part moves to the next stage (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A company produces 5,000 aluminium brackets per week. The quality manager is deciding whether to use 100% inspection with vernier calipers, or a go/no-go gauge sampling system.

Discuss the factors the quality manager should consider when choosing between these two inspection methods.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two relevant factors from both approaches. For example: go/no-go gauges provide fast pass/fail results without operator interpretation, reducing inspection time per part — important at 5,000 per week; however, they do not record the actual dimension, so gradual tool wear drifting towards the tolerance boundary would not be detected until parts fail. Vernier calipers provide actual measurements, enabling trend monitoring (SPC), but are slower and require a skilled operator — at 5,000 parts per week this may create a bottleneck. Both factors developed and linked to the production context.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two factors identified and briefly explained.
Developing (2 marks): One factor on each side but not developed.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A precision engineering company manufactures bearing housings to a bore tolerance of ±0.01 mm. Currently it uses a reactive quality control system, measuring bore diameters at the end of each shift using a micrometer. Defect rates are running at 3%, causing significant scrap costs.

Evaluate the extent to which introducing a quality assurance approach could reduce the company's defect rate and scrap costs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying how QA would address root causes (machine calibration schedules to prevent drift, operator training, approved tooling suppliers), arguing that preventing defects entirely is more cost-effective than detecting them after the part is scrapped, and giving specific examples (e.g. calibrating the boring machine every shift rather than every week could prevent the dimensional drift that produces out-of-tolerance bores). Then challenges this: QA requires investment in time and systems; some variation is inherent and cannot be eliminated by process alone — QC remains necessary to catch the residual defects; and QA systems take time to embed before benefits are seen. A clear judgement is reached — e.g. QA is likely to reduce the 3% defect rate significantly but not to zero; the combination of QA (to address root causes) and reduced-frequency QC (to verify performance) is the optimal approach. Mastering requires the judgement to be substantiated.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both approaches evaluated with some application to the scenario and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is correct regarding the use of gloves near a lathe?
A) Gloves should always be worn to protect the hands from swarf
B) Gloves must not be worn because they can be caught by rotating parts
C) Gloves should be worn only when the machine is running at low speed
D) Gloves are optional if the operator has more than two years' experience
practice_questions.marks: B) Gloves must not be worn because they can be caught by rotating parts [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pieces of PPE that must be worn during a manual arc welding operation.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: welding helmet / auto-darkening shield (to protect against UV radiation) / fire-resistant gloves / leather apron (to protect against burns and spatter) / safety boots with steel toecaps. Do not accept plain safety spectacles alone as these do not protect against UV from the arc. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why PPE is described as the 'last line of defence' in the control hierarchy.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for stating that PPE does not remove or reduce the hazard itself. Second mark: it only protects the individual wearer if the hazard causes an incident — so if the PPE fails or is not worn correctly, the person is unprotected. Third mark: higher-level controls such as machine guards (engineering controls) or safe operating procedures (administrative controls) reduce the hazard for everyone, regardless of individual behaviour, and are therefore more reliable and effective. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the five steps of a risk assessment. Give one example of a control measure for the hazard of swarf during a drilling operation.
practice_questions.marks: Description (3 marks — one per step, award up to 3): identify the hazard; decide who might be harmed and how; evaluate the risk (likelihood × severity); implement control measures; review and update. Example (1 mark): for swarf during drilling — the operator must wear safety spectacles to prevent chips from entering the eyes / a swarf guard should be fitted to the pillar drill to contain chips. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A school engineering workshop runs a risk assessment review after a student cuts their hand on swarf while removing a workpiece from the lathe. The current risk assessment only lists 'wear gloves' as the control measure for swarf.

Discuss whether this control measure is appropriate and what additional measures should be considered.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion that identifies the problem with the current measure (gloves must not be worn near rotating lathes — entanglement risk outweighs the cut risk), then discusses appropriate engineering controls (swarf brush or hook to remove chips rather than bare hands; machine guard during cutting), administrative controls (clear SOP on how to remove swarf safely; supervision; training), and PPE that is appropriate (safety spectacles to prevent chips entering the eyes, rather than gloves). The discussion acknowledges that 'wear gloves' is actively dangerous near rotating machinery — not just ineffective.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two or more relevant points developed and linked to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): Identifies that gloves are inappropriate near lathes but does not develop alternatives.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant safety point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturing company is about to introduce a new process that involves grinding carbon-fibre-reinforced polymer (CRP) components. The process will generate fine airborne particles and significant noise from the grinding machine.

Evaluate how effectively a PPE-only approach would manage the health and safety risks of this new process.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies the specific hazards (fine CRP dust; noise above 85 dB(A); eye hazard from particles), assesses what PPE can offer (FFP3 respirator to filter fine particles; ear defenders; safety spectacles — these address the immediate personal exposure), then critically evaluates the limitations (PPE relies on consistent correct wearing and fit; it does not remove the dust from the environment so other workers nearby are also at risk; hearing protection only works if worn at all times in the noise zone; grinding CRP is a cumulative long-term health risk where any lapse in PPE has lasting consequences). Argues that engineering controls should be primary: local exhaust ventilation (LEV) at the grinding point removes particles before they become airborne; acoustic enclosures reduce noise at source; these protect all workers regardless of individual PPE compliance. Reaches a clear substantiated judgement — PPE is necessary but insufficient alone; LEV and enclosure are essential primary controls.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to CRP grinding context and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or lacking judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about PPE or hazards with little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the main disadvantage of just-in-time (JIT) manufacturing?
A) It requires very large warehouse facilities to store excess components
B) It leads to over-production and excess finished goods
C) A late supplier delivery can stop the entire production line with no buffer stock
D) It prevents manufacturers from using computer-aided production planning
practice_questions.marks: C) A late supplier delivery can stop the entire production line with no buffer stock [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the seven categories of lean waste.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: Transportation / Inventory / Movement / Waiting / Over-processing / Over-production / Defects. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how reducing the waste of 'waiting' can improve manufacturing performance.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that waiting is idle time when operators or machines are not productive. Second mark: by synchronising the output rate of each workstation (balancing the production flow), waiting is eliminated so every stage operates continuously. Third mark: this directly increases throughput — more units are completed per hour without any additional capital investment in machinery. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by material requirements planning (MRP) and give one advantage of using it over ordering materials manually.
practice_questions.marks: Description (2 marks): MRP is a computer-based system that takes the production schedule and, using the bill of materials for each product, calculates exactly what raw materials and components must be ordered, in what quantities, and by what date to ensure production is not delayed (2 marks for a full description; 1 mark for a basic description). Advantage (2 marks): MRP automatically highlights when materials will run short before a stockout actually occurs, allowing the purchasing team to place orders in time to avoid a production stoppage — something that would be difficult to track manually across hundreds of components (2 marks for a developed, applied advantage; 1 mark for a basic statement). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturer of precision components is experiencing high levels of inventory waste and over-production. The production manager wants to introduce lean manufacturing principles.

Discuss the actions the production manager could take to reduce inventory waste and over-production, and the benefits and challenges of doing so.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering specific lean actions for each waste (e.g. introducing pull production / kanban signals for over-production so components are only made when the next stage requests them; implementing JIT ordering to reduce raw material stock for inventory waste), the benefits (reduced capital tied up, more floor space, greater responsiveness), and challenges (requires reliable suppliers for JIT; pull production requires smooth, synchronised production stages — any bottleneck creates waiting; staff need training in the new system). Both wastes addressed with development.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant points developed with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One waste addressed with a basic action.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A car components manufacturer currently operates a traditional push-production system with large raw material and work-in-progress stock holdings. It is considering switching to a full just-in-time system.

Evaluate the extent to which adopting JIT would improve the company's overall manufacturing performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that identifies JIT's genuine performance improvements (eliminated warehousing costs, capital freed from stock holdings, reduced obsolescence risk as components change, faster response to customer demand changes, forces process discipline that often uncovers other inefficiencies), then challenges these with specific risks for this company (car components depend on a complex global supply chain — a single delayed delivery stops the line; the 2021 semiconductor shortage demonstrated how JIT-style supply chains collapse under disruption; initial transition costs are high as supplier contracts and logistics are renegotiated). Reaches a clear substantiated judgement — e.g. JIT would improve cost and responsiveness in stable conditions but creates fragility in the supply chain; a hybrid approach (JIT for high-volume, reliable-supply components; small strategic buffer stocks for high-risk or single-source parts) may be optimal.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to the car components context and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best explains why international standards are important in globalised manufacturing?
A) They allow each country to set its own unique product dimensions
B) They ensure components made in different countries are interchangeable and meet consistent quality requirements
C) They prevent manufacturers from moving production to lower-cost countries
D) They require all manufacturers to use the same machinery and production methods
practice_questions.marks: B) They ensure components made in different countries are interchangeable and meet consistent quality requirements [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two implications of globalisation for employment in the UK manufacturing industry.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: job losses in manufacturing as production moves to lower-cost countries (offshoring) / loss of lower-skill production roles while higher-skill design and management roles may remain / communities dependent on single industries can be severely affected / new employment created in logistics, supply chain management and international trade. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why the transportation required by global supply chains has implications for sustainability.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying that long-distance freight generates carbon emissions. Second mark: air freight in particular emits approximately 50 times more CO₂ per tonne-kilometre than sea freight, making it particularly damaging. Third mark: this conflicts with manufacturers' sustainability targets and national carbon-reduction commitments, particularly when products could be manufactured closer to the end market (reshoring/nearshoring). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what ISO 9001 is and give one benefit to a manufacturing company of achieving ISO 9001 certification.
practice_questions.marks: Description (2 marks): ISO 9001 is an international standard that specifies the requirements for a quality management system — it sets out how a company should control its processes to ensure products consistently meet customer and regulatory requirements (2 marks for a developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'it is a quality standard'). Benefit (2 marks): a company with ISO 9001 certification signals to international customers that its processes meet a recognised global benchmark, opening access to overseas contracts that require certified suppliers — without it the company may be excluded from bidding (2 marks for a specific, developed benefit; 1 mark for a vague answer). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A UK manufacturer of industrial components is considering moving its production to a lower-cost country to reduce manufacturing costs. However, the company has recently committed to a carbon-reduction target.

Discuss the economic and environmental factors the company should consider before making this decision.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering economic factors (lower labour costs in the target country would reduce unit manufacturing cost, potentially improving competitiveness or margins; however, logistics and shipping costs must be added, and supply chain disruption risk increases), and environmental factors (longer supply chain means greater freight emissions, likely by sea but possibly air for urgent orders; manufacturing in a country with weaker environmental regulations may also involve production practices that increase the company's overall environmental footprint; both conflict with the carbon-reduction commitment). Both dimensions developed and linked to the scenario, with some acknowledgement of the tension between them.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two relevant factors identified, briefly explained, some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One factor from each dimension but not developed.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
An international consumer electronics company sources components from manufacturers across Asia, Europe and South America. A recent investigation revealed that some suppliers use excessive working hours and pay below the living wage in their countries.

Evaluate the extent to which a company has a responsibility to ensure ethical employment conditions throughout its global supply chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation that constructs the argument for responsibility (consumers buy the final product believing the company endorses all aspects of its production; the company profits from lower costs partly achieved through poor conditions; reputational risks and, for some UK companies, legal reporting duties under supply chain transparency legislation (e.g. UK Modern Slavery Act); the company has leverage to demand standards as a major customer). Then challenges this: the company cannot directly control independent suppliers in other countries; different legal frameworks mean what is legal abroad may be unacceptable at home; the cost of supply chain auditing is significant; forcing higher wages may make the supply uneconomic and shift production to less-auditable suppliers. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached — e.g. the company has a moral responsibility and may have legal reporting duties, but must act through specific enforceable supplier codes of conduct, regular auditing and willingness to exit relationships with non-compliant suppliers, rather than assuming responsibility can be delegated.
Secure (5–6 marks): Both sides evaluated with some application to the scenario and an attempt at judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development or evaluation. [8 marks]
